title: Food Poisoning, Foodborne Diseases and Food Toxins
shortDescription: Infection vs intoxication vs toxico-infection — and the pathogens exams love.
genZNote: Same plate, three ways to get sick: infection, intoxication, toxico-infection. The exam loves asking which bug uses which mechanism.

sections.heading: Mechanisms
bullets: Food infection: ingestion of live pathogens that multiply in the gut (Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter, Listeria, Vibrio).
Food intoxication: ingestion of preformed toxin (Staphylococcus aureus enterotoxin, Clostridium botulinum, Bacillus cereus emetic).
Toxico-infection: pathogen multiplies and releases toxin in gut (C. perfringens, enterotoxigenic E. coli, V. cholerae, B. cereus diarrhoeal).

table.caption: Pathogen snapshot
rows: Neurotoxin; anaerobic; spores heat-resistant; toxin destroyed by boiling

sections.heading: Food Toxins
bullets: Mycotoxins: aflatoxin B1 (Aspergillus flavus on groundnuts, maize; liver carcinogen; aflatoxin M1 in milk), ochratoxin A, patulin (apple juice), fumonisins, ergot alkaloids.
Marine toxins: ciguatera, paralytic/diarrhoeic shellfish poisoning; scombroid histamine from spoiled tuna/mackerel.
Plant toxins: solanine (green potato), cyanogenic glycosides (cassava, bitter almond), lathyrism toxin, hemagglutinins in raw kidney beans.
Bacterial exotoxins and endotoxins; chemical contaminants such as heavy metals (Pb, Hg, Cd, As) and pesticides.
Prevention: temperature control, hygiene, proper cooking (core 70–75 °C), segregation and safe water; "danger zone" for growth roughly 5–60 °C.

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: Foodborne illness arises from infection, preformed toxin or toxico-infection by bacteria, viruses, parasites, fungi and chemicals.
keyFacts: C. botulinum is anaerobic; toxin is neurotoxin.

commonTraps: Do not classify Salmonella as intoxication.
Do not say reheating removes Staph toxin.

confusedTerms.distinction: Infection needs live organisms; intoxication needs only preformed toxin.
